name: PcapPlusPlus
baseline: libtins v4.5 (C++ packet parsing and crafting library)
workload: Reading and parsing a generated pcap file of 500,000 packets (payload size 742 bytes, three runs averaged) with each library's layer parser: TCP packets without options, TCP with options, and DNS packets (queries and answers counted), using Matias Fontanini's packet-capture-benchmarks suite.
claimed_speedup: Versus libtins v4.5: TCP 0.197 s vs 0.209 s (2,538,071 vs 2,392,344 packets/s), TCP with options 0.202 s vs 0.241 s (2,475,247 vs 2,074,688 packets/s), DNS 0.208 s vs 0.263 s (2,403,846 vs 1,901,140 packets/s), about 1.06x, 1.19x and 1.26x (derived from page data). Not faster than libpcap v1.10.1 on the same page (0.120 s, 0.124 s, 0.031 s), whose loop only counts packets.
compiler_and_flags: g++ 11.4.0 on Ubuntu 22.04 (WSL2); optimization flags for the run are not stated on the page. The suite's Makefile.in builds the PcapPlusPlus benchmark with -g -O2 -std=c++11 and the libtins benchmark with only the configure CXXFLAGS (-std=c++11 plus whatever the user exports).
hardware: Intel Core i7-8700 3.2GHz, 16GB RAM, Windows 10 host running Ubuntu 22.04 in WSL2
tradeoffs: Wraps libpcap, Npcap, WinPcap, DPDK, AF_XDP and PF_RING capture engines and parses 60+ protocols into a layer object model; parsing is lazy per layer, packet objects allocate. Public domain (Unlicense) with no patent grant.
caveats: The win over libtins is small (6 to 26 percent) and a single machine under WSL2 (virtualized) was used. PcapPlusPlus is slower than the raw libpcap loop in all three tests (about 1.6x, 1.6x and 6.7x, derived from page data) because the libpcap benchmark only counts packets without parsing, so libpcap is not a like-for-like baseline. The benchmark.cpp for PcapPlusPlus was copied from the PcapPlusPlus repo and the page was written by its maintainers, so the run is first-party, although the suite and the libtins code come from libtins' author. Times are whole-millisecond averages of 3 runs (the 0.031 s DNS libpcap figure is quantized). Run flags for libtins are not stated and its Makefile build line carries no -O flag. The rendered website page was not opened (egress blocked); numbers were read from its source file in the website repo. The suite repo (mfontanini/packet-capture-benchmarks) has no README or committed results, only scripts.

name: Pistache
baseline: Microsoft C++ REST SDK (cpprestsdk), also Restbed
workload: HTTP GET returning a JSON array of 10,000 items (608,891-byte response), driven by Apache Bench with ab -n 1000 -c 1 -k against 127.0.0.1 inside a Vagrant Ubuntu 16.04 VM, one sequential client.
claimed_speedup: Pistache 319.99 requests/s (3.125 s for 1000 requests) vs Restbed 224.18 requests/s (4.461 s), cpprestsdk with RapidJSON 47.06 requests/s (21.250 s) and cpprestsdk default JSON 30.70 requests/s (32.578 s); PHP 146.95 requests/s. About 1.4x Restbed, 6.8x and 10.4x cpprestsdk (derived from page data). README: '(+) Fastest performance'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmark samples. bootstrap.sh builds RapidJSON, Pistache and Restbed with cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release in the Vagrant box and installs cpprestsdk from the Ubuntu libcpprest-dev package; the sample CMake flags were not read.
tradeoffs: Pre-1.0 and described as unstable on its repo page; the HTTP client component has known issues; Linux, macOS, BSD and Windows support; no inline code documentation per the third-party reviewer.
caveats: Numbers are screenshots of ab output in five PNG files under results/ (benchmark-pistache.png, benchmark-restbed.png, benchmark-cpprestsdk-rapidjson.png, benchmark-cpprestsdk-default_json_impl.png, benchmark-php.png), read by eye; the README text itself has no numbers. The benchmark is a June 2017 snapshot (commits 2017-06-18 to 2017-06-20) taken when Pistache lived at oktal/pistache; one sequential connection, a 600 KB response, one run, host CPU and RAM not stated. The Restbed run shows Keep-Alive requests: 0 so it did not honour -k, which favours Pistache. cpprestsdk's low figures relate to its open issue #468 and an old distro package. The Pistache README makes no speed claim and links a different comparison (guteksan/REST-CPP-benchmark, Pistache v0.0.002 against C++ REST SDK, Crow, HttpLib, Restbed and Restinio, Ubuntu 16.04, 2x14-core Xeon E5-2660 v4) whose own text ranks Pistache in the middle and slightly behind when the thread count is limited, with results only as images that were not read. Treat the claim as weak and dated.

name: POCO FastLogger (Poco::FastLogger, Quill-based)
baseline: Poco::Logger with Poco::AsyncChannel (POCO's existing logging path)
workload: Google Benchmark of calling-thread cost of logging one message to a file, a short message and a long message, comparing Loggers_AsyncChannel_* (Poco::Logger through AsyncChannel) with Loggers_FastLogger_* (Quill lock-free queue plus backend thread), from the Benchmark/ directory added in PR 5081.
claimed_speedup: PR 5081 Linux run: wall time per call 96.3 ns vs 443 ns for the file case (4.6x), 410 ns vs 450 ns short message (1.1x), 621 ns vs 658 ns long message (1.1x); CPU time of the calling thread 12.5 ns vs 434 ns (34.7x), 7.96 ns vs 445 ns (55.9x), 12.3 ns vs 645 ns (52.4x). FastLogger.h comment: 'much lower latency (~9ns vs ~100ns)'.
hardware: Linux, 16 x 2000 MHz CPU (model not stated), load average 2.99 1.19 0.63
tradeoffs: Asynchronous: messages are formatted and written by a backend thread, so output is delayed and can be lost on a crash; FastLogger has no Channel or Formatter objects (configured through a separate fastloggers section); bundles the Quill library and adds about 290 KB to Foundation (can be disabled with -DENABLE_FASTLOGGER=OFF); shipped in POCO 1.15.0.
caveats: First-party claim by a POCO maintainer. The large multipliers are CPU time of the calling thread only, which leaves out backend-thread formatting and I/O; the wall-time gain for short and long messages is only about 1.1x. Compiler, flags and CPU model are not stated in the PR (only '16 X 2000 MHz CPU s'); the benchmark code is public in Benchmark/src/LoggerBench.cpp. The '~9ns vs ~100ns' comment has no stated methodology. The baseline is POCO's own logging path, not a third-party logger, and POCO's HTTP and networking components (the listed seed) have no comparative numbers anywhere reached. Other PR numbers (macOS, Windows) were not extracted.
